content.text: Electromagnetic waves have transformed our world. From the radio in your car to the X-ray at the dentist, from the remote control in your hand to the satellite above your head—EM waves are everywhere. This lesson explores the practical applications of each type of electromagnetic radiation.
Signals transmitted from transmitters to receivers
Signal used to modulate a carrier wave
Receiver picks up signal and converts back
Use radio waves to communicate with base stations
Radio telescopes detect radio waves from space:
Microwaves absorbed by water molecules in food
Food heats from within (not just surface)
Higher frequency microwaves for mobile networks

Each type of EM wave has specific uses based on its properties. The uses depend on wavelength, energy, penetrating power, and how different materials interact with that type of radiation.
Infrared light used for data transmission
Total internal reflection keeps light in fibre
Faster than electrical signals in wires

UV light damages DNA of bacteria and viruses
Used to sterilise: water, medical equipment, surfaces
Invisible ink visible under UV light
Hand stamps visible under UV "black lights"

Diagnose fractures, dental problems, joint issues
Multiple X-ray images from different angles

When asked about dangers of EM waves, always link the danger to the type of radiation: ionising radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma) can damage DNA and cause cancer; microwaves and infrared cause heating of body tissue.
Careful planning minimises damage to healthy tissue

— They penetrate a few centimetres and heat water wherever they're absorbed. Deep parts are heated by conduction.
— Controlled UV exposure produces vitamin D and treats some skin conditions.
— Gamma irradiation sterilises food but doesn't make it radioactive.
"X-rays are safe because they're just for bones"
— X-rays are ionising and carry risks; exposure should be minimised.
"Mobile phones use radio waves, so they're completely safe"
— Current evidence suggests normal use is safe, but research continues.

Each type has specific properties that make it suitable for particular applications
Some applications require waves to penetrate materials; others require absorption
Hazardous waves (UV, X-rays, gamma) are used carefully with appropriate safety measures
Microwaves can pass through the atmosphere

and travel in straight lines to and from satellites in orbit; their shorter wavelength allows them to carry more data. Radio waves (FM) are used for local broadcasting because they can cover a wide area from a ground-based transmitter but do not penetrate the ionosphere as effectively for satellite links. (comparison)
Infrared requires a roughly line-of-sight path

between the remote and the receiver. IR radiation cannot pass through solid objects (walls, furniture) and does not diffract significantly around obstacles because its wavelength is very short compared to everyday objects. (reasoning)
Bones are dense and absorb X-rays
, creating a clear white shadow on the image. Soft-tissue organs transmit X-rays in similar amounts to surrounding tissue, so there is insufficient contrast to form a useful image. (comparison)
remote controls and thermal imaging cameras (recall) b)
sterilisation of water/equipment and security marking on banknotes (recall)
All warm objects emit infrared radiation.
A thermal imaging camera has sensors that detect IR and convert the varying intensities into a colour-coded image, where hotter areas appear as brighter/different colours. (description)
Gamma rays have much higher energy per photon

than visible light. This energy is sufficient to damage the DNA of bacteria and other microorganisms, killing them. Visible light does not have enough energy to achieve this sterilisation effect. Gamma rays also penetrate sealed packaging. (comparison)
Data is encoded as pulses of infrared or visible light.

These pulses enter a thin glass or plastic fibre and travel along it by total internal reflection, bouncing off the inner walls at angles greater than the critical angle. This allows signals to travel long distances with very little energy loss. (description)
